extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research funders, policy‑makers and administrators interested in the evidence base and reform of grant peer review (e.g., CIHR review panels, funder evaluators)
extracted.subtask_description: A literature‑review style evaluation of the effectiveness, reliability, fairness, burden and accountability of peer review as a mechanism for awarding grant funding in the health sciences, and suggested reforms for funders and panels. Focuses on empirical evidence, biases, costs and procedural remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is probably anti-innovation; reviewers tend to under-score novel or high‑risk proposals, and low success rates may push applicants and reviewers to be conservative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations suggested include using reviewers with different cognitive biases for schemes targeting high‑risk research, making 'innovation' an assessment criterion, increasing the weight given to innovation, using disagreement among reviewers to flag novel work, and investigator‑focused funding (selecting researchers on merit) or Delphi processes. Caution: panels may lack expertise to assess innovation and increasing emphasis on impact can disadvantage innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary research fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not clear if peer review treats interdisciplinary research fairly; interdisciplinary reviews must combine distinct understandings of 'quality' and it can be difficult to find suitable peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested remedies: increase panel size, broaden range of expertise/disciplines, diminish role of single in‑depth initial reviewers. Trade‑off: increasing panel breadth increases burden and may reduce consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translational/applied research fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review may inhibit translational and applied health research; applied researchers may get less credit due to publishing in specialist/lower‑impact journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include research users on panels, consider likely impact in funding decisions (merit review panels combining academic and user/policy communities). Note: considering impact at application stage can disadvantage innovation; evidence is limited and mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity (weak predictor of future performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is at best only a weak predictor of future research performance (bibliometric and other follow‑up measures show little or weak association with grant scores).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bibliometrics are imperfect proxies, but multiple studies found weak correlation between percentile ranking and later bibliometric performance. Funders should acknowledge uncertainty and consider alternative signals (e.g., score distributions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability — inter-rater agreement and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratings vary considerably between reviewers; single‑rater reliabilities are low (examples: correlations ~0.19–0.23), with conflicting evidence on whether overall decision consistency is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible improvements: better reviewer training, use of mean reviewer scores as a practical alternative to lengthy panel re‑ratings, evaluation of review quality, triage rather than re‑rating, and measures such as intra‑class correlation. Expectations: Bornmann suggested 80–90% agreement as a target; empirical rates vary widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — gender bias
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a substantial and conflicting body of evidence on gender bias; some analyses suggest men are modestly more likely to be funded (e.g., 7% advantage in a meta‑analysis), while other large studies find no bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting aggregate effects is complex; cohort effects and field differences matter. Funders may need targeted analyses and policies (e.g., anonymisation, monitoring) but evidence is mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — age bias and early career disadvantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence is conflicting on age bias; some studies show declines in scores/selection with age or lower early career success rates, others find no direct age effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns are tied to reliance on prior publications/funding; funders have used measures to equalise success rates for new investigators (e.g., NIH policies). Monitoring and tailored schemes for early career researchers recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — cronyism and institutional bias
rubrics_metrics.description: There is evidence peer review suffers from cronyism: prior affiliation with reviewers or institutional prestige can increase funding chances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should have detailed conflict of interest processes and consider blinding/anonymisation where feasible, though anonymisation may be imperfect; panel composition and rules to reduce nepotism are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — cognitive particularism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may favour proposals aligned with their own field or school of thought ('cognitive particularism'), which can disadvantage cross‑disciplinary or novel approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that panel makeup influences outcomes; use broader expertise, conflict‑of‑interest rules, or alternative assessment methods to counteract particularism. Evidence on the prevalence is mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and transparency (review anonymity trade-offs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review anonymity reduces transparency; blinding of applications can defend against biases but may be imperfect and reduce accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some funders attempt anonymisation before review, but identification can persist from content. Balance transparency, accountability and feasibility when designing blinding policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness — speed of funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can slow down the grant award process detrimentally, making it not timely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider process redesigns (e.g., short proposals, accelerated review, virtual panels) to reduce delays; weigh timeliness against thoroughness and other objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder confidence in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review may lack the confidence of key stakeholders; it is not always the preferred method of resource allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should survey and consider stakeholder views and be prepared to trial alternative methods and increase transparency to build confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of peer review on the research system
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of peer review is high and increasing; around 75% of the burden falls on applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efforts to reduce burden have often focused on funders/reviewers, but applicant costs/time must be recognised and measured (e.g., time and monetary costs of preparing NIH proposals). Consider shorter applications, triage, and other streamlining approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of burden (applicants vs funders/reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the burden falls on applicants (~75%); many burden‑reduction efforts target funders and reviewers rather than applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reforms that reduce applicant time (short proposals, triage, accelerated review) and transparently measure who bears costs of processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reviewers’ uncertainty/score distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders should acknowledge and analyse uncertainty around peer review — for example using reviewers’ uncertainty or the distribution of scores as inputs to funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High disagreement between reviewers could be taken as an indicator of potentially innovative/high‑risk work; funders could exploit disagreement rather than treat it as noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random allocation / lottery element
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider introducing a lottery element in some parts of the funding allocation process to reduce both burden and bias, and to allow better evaluation of decision processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random allocation has been used in some schemes (e.g., NZ Health Research Council) and can be experimental; weigh acceptability and impact on perceived fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training (NIH suggested training items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve reviewer performance via training focusing on: (1) emphasising strengths rather than weaknesses; (2) focusing on potential impact; (3) reviewing merit and not re‑writing proposals; (4) recognising implicit bias; (5) using benchmark applications during panel meetings; (6) pointing out bias towards lesser‑known organisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief training programmes have been shown to increase inter‑rater reliability (example: increase from 0.61 to 0.89) but may increase time spent reviewing. Implement and evaluate training carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Many funders evaluate the quality of reviews using criteria such as completeness, level of substantiation, appropriateness, comprehensibility, timeliness and usefulness, and may return or reject poor reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating review quality can improve review standards but adds burden. No strong empirical data quantify the effect; sampling reviews vs full evaluation shows little difference per funder surveys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel meeting impact vs mean reviewer scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel discussion typically changes funding decisions for a minority (~10%) of applications; mean pre‑meeting reviewer scores may be a practical and economical alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies show minimal differences between face‑to‑face and teleconference panels, and that consensus meetings often yield little net change. Consider cost/benefit of full panel meetings vs statistical aggregation of scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtual panels vs face-to-face
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleconference and videoconference panels produce similar scoring distributions to face‑to‑face panels, although participants value in‑person social interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtual formats can reduce costs; consider participant preferences and potential effects on deliberation when choosing mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage and multi-stage review
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial triage of applications may be preferable to re‑rating rounds because panel discussion rarely moves applications across decision thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design multi‑stage processes to limit unnecessary re‑scoring; dependent reliability can be high but whole‑population effects may be limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition diversity effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing diversity of background and discipline among reviewers reduces rating consistency; agreement is lower among experts from different disciplines or from research/practice/policy backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While diversity may improve fairness for interdisciplinary topics, expect reduced inter‑rater reliability; balance disciplinary representation with decision consistency and burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel size and breadth of expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing panel size and breadth of expertise has been suggested to address interdisciplinarity, but this increases burden and may only work if the role of initial in‑depth reviewers is reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade‑off analysis required: larger panels may reduce bias against interdisciplinarity but increase cost and coordination complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding/anonymisation of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Blinding proposals can reduce bias (gender, institutional) but anonymisation is often imperfect and reviewers can sometimes infer applicant identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement blinding cautiously; evaluate its effectiveness and consider complementary measures (e.g., conflict of interest rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest management
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders maintain detailed conflict‑of‑interest processes to counter real or perceived cronyism, but strict rules may exclude the most knowledgeable reviewers in small fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the need to avoid nepotism with ensuring sufficient expertise; transparency and clear COI policies are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using reviewer disagreement as innovation signal
rubrics_metrics.description: High disagreement among reviewers might identify potentially innovative or high‑risk/high‑reward proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders could treat divergence in scores as an informative signal rather than noise, and design pathways (e.g., special funding streams) for such proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting researchers on merit (investigator-based funding)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative is to select researchers on merit regardless of proposed projects, giving them freedom to pursue novel ideas (example: MacArthur Fellows model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May sidestep conservatism against innovation, but represents a substantial shift in funding philosophy and requires methods to define and assess 'merit'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delphi process for situations with limited evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a structured, deliberative Delphi process could help assess research merits when scientific evidence is limited and panel opinions diverge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delphi has been found efficient and flexible and may improve consensus where standard peer review struggles; evaluate time/cost trade‑offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make 'innovation' an explicit assessment criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Some funders have made 'innovation' an explicit criterion; evidence on effectiveness is mixed and panels may lack expertise to judge innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider training reviewers to assess innovation, use benchmark examples, and monitor correlations between innovation scores and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funders should experiment and share data
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need for open, transparent experimentation and evaluation of different ways to fund research; funders should make data available to allow better study of allocation processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage controlled trials (e.g., lotteries, alternative review models), data sharing, and independent evaluation to build evidence for reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: GRADE evidence quality scale (for studies of peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of evidence was rated on a scale based on GRADE: 1 Assumptions (intuitive beliefs); 2 Suggestive; 3 Conflicting; 4 Agreement; 5 Compelling (systematic reviews are compelling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this scale to qualify strength of empirical findings about peer review issues; many topics in the literature are suggestive or conflicting rather than compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature review inclusion/exclusion criteria (methodological standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: For this review, studies were included if they provided empirical consideration of effectiveness and/or burden of grant review processes and were from 2009 onwards; excluded were purely descriptive accounts, manuscript peer review studies, reviews summarising pre-2008 work, and items without additional synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or conducting literature reviews on grant peer review, apply clear inclusion/exclusion rules, document search strategies, and capture key study information systematically (e.g., Excel extraction).
